Definition 1. Let G = (V, E) be an undirected graph. A cut in G is a partition
of V into two non-empty subsets S and V \ S. The set of edges between S and
V \S is called the edge cut induced by (S, V \S). A cut is minimal if no proper
subset of its edge cut forms a valid cut in G.
Lemma 1. Every non-empty edge cut contains at least one minimal edge cut.
Proof. Let C be a non-empty edge cut corresponding to partition (S, V \ S).
Consider all edge cuts contained in C ordered by inclusion. By Zorn’s Lemma,
there exists a minimal element in this partially ordered set, which is a minimal
edge cut contained in C.
Lemma 2. If C1 and C2 are minimal edge cuts with C1∩C2 ̸= ∅, then C1 = C2.
Proof. Suppose C1 ̸= C2 but C1 ∩C2 ̸= ∅. Then C1 ∩C2 would be a proper
subset of both C1 and C2 that still separates the graph (since both C1 and C2
separate the graph and they share edges). This contradicts the minimality of
C1 and C2.
Theorem 1. Every edge cut in G can be expressed as a disjoint union of min-
imal edge cuts.
Proof. Let C be an arbitrary edge cut in G. We proceed by induction on the
size of C.
Base case: If |C| = 1, then C is trivially a minimal cut and the theorem
holds.
Inductive step: Assume the theorem holds for all edge cuts of size less
than n. Consider an edge cut C with |C| = n.
By Lemma 1, C contains at least one minimal edge cut C1. Let C′ = C \C1.
Then C′ is either empty (in which case we’re done) or is itself an edge cut:
If C′ separates the graph, then by the inductive hypothesis, C′ can be written
as a disjoint union of minimal cuts Sk
i=2 Ci. Since C1 was chosen to be minimal
and C1 ∩Ci = ∅for all i ≥2 (by Lemma 2), we have C = Sk
i=1 Ci as a disjoint
union.
If C′ does not separate the graph, then C1 must contain all edges between
some components of G \ C′, meaning C′ wasn’t actually an edge cut to begin
with. This contradicts our initial assumption, so this case cannot occur.
Thus, by induction, the theorem holds for all edge cuts.
